chapter_theme: Gambling is ruin even when it pays, because a win is the bait that holds the player. It takes wealth first, then truthfulness, compassion and the basics of living, and the attachment grows with each loss.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: it brings poverty (931-935), it does many small harms and ruins both worlds (936-939), and it is hard to quit, which shows the greatness of those who do (940).

931.reading: Don't want gambling even if you can win, for what you win is like the metal of the hook swallowed by a fish.
931.nuance: The verse attacks gambling at its strongest case, a win. Parimelazhagar adds that the winnings are a shackle keeping the gambler from leaving. பொன் here means the hook's metal, not gold, though the sound of 'gold' sharpens the image.

932.reading: Is there any way of living well for gamblers, who get one and lose a hundred?
932.nuance: ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் is sequence as well as ratio. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar hear the hope that follows the first gain, so the loss is driven by the win.

933.reading: If one keeps calling the falling of the dice, the gains of wealth will leave and pass elsewhere.
933.nuance: The chiming of உருளாயம் and பொருளாயம் sets one income against another: the income of the dice swallows the income of wealth. Parimelazhagar makes the subject a king and the destination his enemies, which the verse doesn't state.

934.reading: There is nothing that gives poverty like gambling, which does many small harms and destroys distinction.
934.nuance: சிறுமை elsewhere is smallness of character. The commentators read it here as miseries, but both senses are available, since gambling diminishes a person as well as afflicting him.

935.reading: Those who, in pride, clung to the dice, the gaming hall and the skilled hand have come to nothing.
935.nuance: The past tense makes this an appeal to history. Parimelazhagar names the example: the Pandavas losing their kingdom and going to the forest. The verse names no one, so this epic reference is his.

936.reading: Those covered by the goddess of misfortune named gambling will not fill themselves and will suffer distress.

positions.position: அகடு is the belly: they go hungry here, and suffer hell in the next world.
positions.quote: இம்மைக்கண் வயிறாரப் பெறார்; மறுமைக்கண் நிரயத் துன்பம் உழப்பர்.

positions.position: அகடு is what lies within, the senses and the mind, which are never satisfied, and the covering hides their good qualities.
positions.quote: தமக்கு உள்ளாகிய இந்திரியங்களும் மனமும் இன்புற்று நிறை யப்பெறார்

937.reading: If காலை enters the gaming hall, it will ruin long-held wealth and character.
937.nuance: Whichever reading is taken, time is the stake, not money: ruin comes from what the hours would have been spent on.

positions.position: காலை means the time set apart for virtue, wealth and pleasure, especially a king's.
positions.quote: அறம் பொருள் இன்பங்கட்கு அடைத்த காலம் அரசனுக்குச் சூதாடு களத்தின்கண் கழியுமாயின்

938.reading: Gambling destroys wealth, makes one take up lying, destroys compassion and drives one through misery.
938.nuance: The list is a causal ladder, and the moral rungs come after the financial one. Parimelazhagar assigns the means: loss robs, the winner's position breeds lies, and the rancour of the game kills compassion. In his reading, then, wins and losses alike do damage.

939.reading: Clothing, wealth, food, lustre and learning, these five don't come near one who takes to gaming.
939.nuance: அடையாவாம் says that they won't arrive, while Pope's 'depart' adds that they were held already. The list runs from bare needs to learning, and puts survival and culture under one head.

940.reading: As a gambler loves the game more with every loss, so the living being's love grows with every suffering it goes through.
940.nuance: An unexpected turn to the human condition: the chapter's closing verse uses gambling to diagnose attachment to life itself. Parimelazhagar insists the real target is the gambler, with the soul there to drive the point home, but the verse's grammar makes the soul the thing explained.

positions.position: The soul's love is for the body, through which it suffers; as the one quitting gambling is admired, so is the soul that spurns the body.
positions.quote: சூதினை வெறுத்து ஒழிவானை யொக்கும் உடம்பினை வெறுத்தொழியும் உயிர்

positions.position: The love is for life itself, which grows as the body suffers; no renunciation is implied.

links.note: Under Parimelazhagar's reading of 940 the two are one argument: the soul clings to the body through suffering as a gambler clings through loss, and 345 says that for those ending birth even the body is one attachment too many. 940 is the disease and 345 the cure.

Both use முகடி, the goddess of misfortune. 617 lodges her in idleness and 936 equates her with gambling. Parimelazhagar's remark on 936 that her name is too ill-omened to say makes gambling her acceptable alias.
The hook's bait in 931 becomes the mechanism in 932: the one small win pulls the hundred losses after it. Parimelazhagar explicitly ties them together with அத்தூண்டிற் பொன்.

source_issues: 939, 940: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
932: Parimelazhagar's lemma reads ஒன்று உய்தி where the verse has ஒன்றெய்தி, apparently a transcription error.
933: Manakkudavar's text ends with a stray digit 4.
936: Pope's gloss has 'pangs of hell in the next world' from Parimelazhagar; the verse says only அல்லல் உழப்பர்.
938: the Parimelazhagar text records a variant reading, பொருள் கொடுத்து.
